title: Rabies Control Cannot Stop at Vietnam’s Household Gates
excerpt: On 7 September 2026, a dog in Đắk Lắk tested positive for rabies after biting four people. Separately, uninspected animal transport and slaughter create severe biosecurity risks.
body_html:
On 7 September 2026 in Đắk Lắk, a domestic dog tested positive for rabies virus after biting four people, according to Tuổi Trẻ. All four victims received prompt post-exposure prophylaxis. The incident illustrates a stark reality: rabies control cannot stop at household gates.

Rabies Prevention Starts With Vaccination and Prompt Treatment

Rabies spreads primarily through saliva from infected animal bites or scratches. Once clinical symptoms develop, the virus is virtually 100% fatal. Anyone bitten, scratched, or otherwise potentially exposed should immediately wash and flush affected wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, then seek urgent medical assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis, including rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin when indicated. Do not wait for symptoms. Seek care even if time has passed since exposure. Vietnam’s reported burden remains severe: by 3 September 2026, authorities recorded 164 animal rabies outbreaks across 129 communes, wards, and townships in 22 provinces and cities, with 51 human deaths reported nationwide, according to reported veterinary and public-health figures.

This household case does not establish any direct connection to the commercial dog-meat trade. Separately, however, inadequate vaccination and the absence of veterinary controls during animal transport and slaughter create preventable exposure risks across informal supply chains. Animals move across provincial borders without verified ownership, vaccination certificates, or quarantine inspections. Handlers and slaughterhouse workers face dangerous, preventable risks through bites, scratches, and contact with infectious saliva or neural tissues on broken skin or mucous membranes. These systemic gaps demonstrate why an informal, underground animal trade is an unacceptable public health hazard.

Dog Theft and the Illicit Supply Chain

On 9 September 2026, TAND khu vực 3 Tây Ninh sentenced Nguyễn Thanh Xuân to four years in prison and Phan Trung Chánh to two years for dog theft, and Đoàn Thị Lương to one year for illegal resale. When authorities intercepted the group on 8 January 2026, they seized 19 live stolen dogs; court records documented more than 1.6 tonnes of dogs trafficked through the operation, according to Báo Tây Ninh. These convictions deliver justice to targeted pet owners while demonstrating how stolen animals are funneled through illicit trade and resale networks.

Public sentiment strongly supports reform. A 2021 nationwide survey commissioned by Four Paws found that 95% of Vietnamese respondents supported ending the dog and cat meat trade. Companion animals are widely cherished by owners as household protectors and friends rather than commodities for trafficking.

From Public Health Safeguards to Total Abolition

Universal pet registration, mandatory rabies vaccination, provincial transport checkpoints, and criminal penalties for pet theft are vital immediate safeguards. But in our campaign’s view, regulating an informal, high-risk trade cannot eliminate its inherent hazards. While Vietnam’s National Program for Rabies Control and Elimination pursues public-health targets to reduce human fatalities, biosecurity cannot be guaranteed while an illicit companion-animal trade continues to operate.

Our campaign demands a definitive legislative endpoint: the total nationwide abolition of dog-meat slaughter, trade, and consumption by 2030. Sign the national petition. Demand strict traceability now. Demand relentless enforcement against pet theft now. Demand complete abolition by 2030.
